newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Angola force renewal recommended until Feb. 28.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Angola force renewal recommended until Feb. 28.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali recommended on Thursday that the current U.N. peacekeeping operation in Angola be extended until Feb. 28, 1997, with the progressive withdrawal of troops to be completed by the end of July or August.

The U.N. Angola Verification Mission (UNAVEM III), which numbers 7,000 troops and military observers, has been monitoring the implementation of an agreement signed in Lusaka, Zambia, in November 1994, ending nearly two decades of civil war between the Angolan government and the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA).
The current mandate of UNAVEM III, the biggest U.N. peacekeeping operation, costing some $300 million a year, expires on Dec. 11.
When it was set up in February 1995 it had been expected to last two years and the wind-down of the force has begun.

In a report to the Security Council, Boutros-Ghali recommended that the withdrawal of military units resume in February 1997, "with a view to a complete drawdown within a period of six to seven months."

He said he planned to repatriate by mid-June 1997 four of the force's six infantry battalions, together with support units and some military headquarters personnel, "with the remainder of the formed units to be repatriated by the end of July or August 1997."

A rapid reaction force comprising six company-sized infantry groups should be retained until completion of the withdrawal of all military contingents, unless political and security conditions permitted a faster drawdown.

Boutros-Ghali said the activities of UNAVEM III would be increasingly concentrated on political, police and human rights monitoring, humanitarian activities including demining, as well as public information and logistical support.
"In the meantime, and having in mind the considerations presented above, I recommend that the present mandate of UNAVEM III be extended until February 28, 1997," he said.
Meanwhile, implementation of the Lusaka Protocol "continues to proceed in fits and starts, often only after increased pressure has been applied on the parties," he said.

"This unsatisfactory situation cannot continue," he added, appealing to the Angolan government and UNITA to resolve key outstanding issues before January 1, 1997. These include the return to Luanda of UNITA deputies to the National Assembly, establishment of a government of national unity and reconciliation, and agreement on the special status of the leader of the largest opposition party.

"Further procrastination in resolving these issues may negatively affect both the peace process and the willingness of the international community to maintain its extensive involvement in Angola," Boutros-Ghali said.
